written.myAnswer: Metals generally lose their outer electrons easily; non-metals generally gain electrons easily.
They usually have weak intermolecular attractions between their molecules, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules.
Diamond is an example of a crystalline solid whose carbon atoms are joined by covalent bonds.
Metallic bonds are non-directional, allowing layers of metal atoms to slide past one another without the bonding being broken; this makes metals malleable and ductile.
Yes. Once formed, a coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond and is generally strong.
A Lewis structure can be written as H–O–N(=O)→O, with the coordinate bond shown from N to the terminal O; include the appropriate lone pairs and formal charges in the dot-and-cross diagram.

HF has a much higher boiling point than HCl because HF molecules form hydrogen bonds, whereas HCl molecules have weaker intermolecular attractions. However, at ordinary room temperature HF is also a gas (its boiling point is about 19.5 °C); it is not a liquid.
Most covalent compounds are non-polar, while water is polar, so they generally do not dissolve in water.
Mobile electrons transfer kinetic energy through the metal, allowing metals to conduct heat.
Five common oxides are N₂O, NO, N₂O₃, NO₂ and N₂O₅.
AgBr forms as a pale-yellow (cream) precipitate, while NaNO₃ remains dissolved: NaBr(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgBr(s) + NaNO₃(aq).
I₂ molecules are larger and more polarizable than Cl₂ molecules, so their intermolecular attractions are stronger. Iodine is solid while chlorine is a gas at room temperature.
An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer. A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions form a regular three-dimensional ionic lattice. Each ion is surrounded by six oppositely charged ions.

Metallic bonding consists of positive metal ions attracted to delocalised electrons. The mobile electrons allow electrical and thermal conductivity, while the non-directional attraction allows malleability and ductility. Strong metallic bonding often gives metals high melting points.

Ionic compounds are usually crystalline solids with high melting points; they conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water and are often water-soluble. Covalent compounds generally have lower melting and boiling points, usually do not conduct electricity, and are often insoluble in water.
Each carbon atom in graphite forms covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms. The remaining electrons are delocalised and can move through the layers, carrying electrical charge.

Strong metallic attraction holds metal atoms or ions together in a closely packed structure, making metals generally hard. Their often high density means a given volume has considerable mass, making them feel heavy.
In Al₂Cl₆, chlorine atoms bridge the two AlCl₃ units. A lone pair from each bridging chlorine is donated to an electron-deficient aluminium atom, forming coordinate covalent bonds.
Sand (quartz, SiO₂) has a giant three-dimensional covalent network. Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom is shared between two silicon atoms.
